sources.news_title: Tucker Carlson Warns Netanyahu Is Calling Trump 'Every Day' as Iran Strikes Resume and Sen. Murphy’s ‘Insane’ Warning Suddenly Looks Prophetic
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s administration launched a new round of limited strikes on Iranian targets on the eve of today’s midterm elections. The military action comes as conservative commentator Tucker Carlson alleges that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch a nuclear strike against Iran, raising questions about the potential for further escalation.
The developments come days after Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy warned that the administration’s military plans were “insane” and predicted devastating consequences. Two days later, Murphy suffered a stroke and was hospitalized.
Now, with Netanyahu reportedly urging Trump to intensify the military campaign and Carlson warning of a possible nuclear strike, the question is no longer simply whether the United States will launch additional attacks on Iran, but how far the president might be willing to escalate the conflict.
According to The Associated Press, American forces struck Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, hours before voters headed to the polls.
A U.S. official said the limited operation targeted Iranian forces using surface-to-air missiles against American personnel. The official spoke anonymously because they lacked authorization to comment publicly. The strikes followed weeks of speculation about whether Trump would resume a broader military campaign after Election Day.
The timing is particularly significant because Netanyahu reportedly pressed Trump for renewed strikes during a weekend telephone conversation, according to regional officials and another person familiar with the discussion, the AP reported.
Trump acknowledged speaking with Netanyahu, describing their conversation as “very good,” but offered few details.
That confirmed contact has given new relevance to allegations Carlson made Sunday night, when he claimed Netanyahu was pushing Trump toward a far more consequential military decision.
In a lengthy post on X, Carlson alleged that Netanyahu wanted the United States to use a nuclear weapon against Pickaxe Mountain, an underground Iranian facility that reportedly lies beneath hundreds of feet of rock.
“Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” Carlson wrote, quoting an unnamed observer.
Carlson claimed conventional American weapons could not penetrate the mountain’s protective granite. He said Netanyahu was pressing for a nuclear strike as the only way to destroy infrastructure he believes could enrich uranium.
He further alleged that Trump could make a decision by Nov. 7, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff were pushing for a diplomatic settlement.
Those allegations have not been independently verified. The White House has dismissed Carlson’s account, and no public evidence establishes that Trump is considering using a nuclear weapon.
But the underlying military problem Carlson described is not entirely imaginary.
A Newsweek analysis examined the difficulty of destroying Pickaxe Mountain’s deeply buried infrastructure, raising the possibility that conventional weapons might be insufficient to eliminate the entire facility.
That does not establish that nuclear weapons are necessary, much less that the administration intends to use them. Destroying a facility completely and rendering it temporarily inoperable are different military objectives.
Trump himself discussed Pickaxe Mountain during a Monday appearance on Fox News, suggesting the United States could deal with the site quickly.
The president’s remarks came as diplomatic negotiations continued, with U.S. and regional officials working to reach an agreement that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and prevent a return to full-scale fighting.
For Murphy, the danger of escalation was already apparent before the latest developments.
Speaking Thursday about a classified Pentagon briefing, the Connecticut Democrat warned that the administration was contemplating a short military operation with potentially catastrophic consequences.
“You’ve heard a preview that it would be a short-duration plan. I will just say this: Their plan is insane,” Murphy said.
“It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.”
Two days later, Murphy, 53, experienced numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game. He was taken to the hospital, where doctors determined he had suffered a stroke.
His chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said Sunday that Murphy was awake, alert and responding well to treatment at Johns Hopkins Hospital. She added that doctors were encouraged by his progress and optimistic about his full recovery.
The timing of Murphy’s warning and subsequent hospitalization sparked speculation online. However, there is no evidence linking his stroke to his criticism of Trump or the administration’s Iran policy.

sources.text:
The U.S. Has Been Striking Iran as Trump Talks Up a Deal
Trump posted that oil was crashing because Iran wants peace, then US officials said American jets had just struck Iranian territory. The two stories cannot both be true, and oil traders are now betting on which one to believe.
At 3:46 p.m. ET on Monday, November 2, 2026, President Trump posted on Truth Social: “Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”
Later that day, US officials said American forces had hit Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. They described it as the latest in a series of limited strikes that the Pentagon has not announced. For anyone who owns oil, the two signals point in opposite directions.
Trump’s claim overstated the day. Brent fell $8.66, or 7.63%, to $104.77, and WTI fell $7.66, or 7.36%, to $96.46. Neither came close to the April 8 record.
Stocks closed before the strike report came out. United States Oil Fund (NYSEARCA:USO) fell 7.08% to $156.87, and Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) fell 4.05% to $179.67.
What Officials Said and What Nobody Confirmed
The only source for the strikes is unnamed US officials. The Pentagon sent questions to US Central Command, and Iranian authorities have confirmed nothing, although Iranian state media reported several explosions on the island.
A senior official said one US fighter jet destroyed one surface-to-air missile launcher in self-defense after the Revolutionary Guards fired a missile from it. Nobody has verified any damage or casualty count.
Earlier, reporters asked Trump whether he was considering strikes after the November 3 midterms. He said “no” and added, “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.” He made those remarks before the strike report came out.
Vice President JD Vance said he and Trump “feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” but they have not set a deadline. A diplomat said a draft deal would have Iran quickly reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for US sanctions relief. No text has been released.
Why Oil Barely Moved on the Strike Report
After the report, Brent rose 0.5% to $105.25, and WTI rose 0.5% to $96.93 in early Asian trading. The small move suggests the market is focused on whether the strait reopens. Before the war began on February 28, nearly 20% of the world’s oil supply passed through it.
Pavel Molchanov of Raymond James said the “false dawns” of recent months warrant caution. The real record drop came on April 8. That day WTI fell more than 16%, or roughly $18, to $94.43, and Brent fell over 13%, or roughly $14, to $94.75.
Exxon Can Handle a Deal Better Than USO
USO owns front-month WTI futures contracts. Each time a contract expires, it has to buy the next one, and that roll costs money, so over time the fund drifts away from the price of crude. It traded at $157.75 after hours, up 0.56%.
Exxon is worth $732.87 billion. It also refines fuel and makes chemicals, and it plans $20 billion in share buybacks in 2027. Those businesses help offset lower crude prices. The stock traded at $179.90 after hours, up 0.13%.
Chevron (NYSE:CVX) is worth $444.38 billion, and fell 3.29% to $227.77 before edging up 0.21% to $228.25 after hours.
Goldman Sachs projects that Brent could reach $140 in 2027 if Gulf oil output stays 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average.
The national average for regular gasoline was $4.1694. That is down from $4.2858 a week earlier but well above $3.0361 a year earlier, which keeps pressure on the White House to get a deal done.
How USO and Exxon Could Respond to a Hormuz Deal
USO has the most direct exposure to a deal. USO is up 126.82% year to date. A signed deal would hurt a futures fund the most, and roll costs keep cutting into returns over time.
Exxon has more buffer than USO. Its refining margins, its 2.35% dividend yield, and 44 straight years of dividend increases provide income to shareholders while the talks continue.
Keep an eye on whether Brent closes below the April 8 level of $94.75, and also on whether there is a confirmed Hormuz reopening, actual sanctions relief, or official confirmation of the strikes.

While President Donald Trump touted the possibility of a peace deal, the U.S. conducted a series of strikes against Iran.
Qeshm Island, an island at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, that is home to an underground missile site and Iranian Navy Base, was struck on Monday, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal on Monday. This was the latest in a series of strikes that the U.S. launched against Iran over the past several weeks.
These strikes occurred while Trump downplayed the nature of the ongoing Iran war, falsely claiming that the U.S. “won.”
🚨 FAFO: Iran fired a missile at an American aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz. Then it found out.
A U.S. fighter jet DESTROYED the IRGC missile launcher on Qeshm Island in self-defense, U.S. officials say.
Officials call it limited and defensive. It is not a return to war.
Talks are still going. JD Vance says he and Trump feel good about a deal, but the president keeps every option open.
Trump warns Iran will get “the hammer” if the talks fail.
Peace through STRENGTH. That is how you do it.
— Gunther Eagleman™ (@GuntherEagleman) November 3, 2026

The United States Central Command (CENTCOM) did not immediately respond for comment.
The strikes were limited, small scale defensive measures intended to prevent Iran from attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, United States officials told the New York Times.
In one instance, Iranians fired a missile at an American fighter jet in self-defense. In another confrontation, United States forces intercepted a missile that originated in Qeshm Island that was targeting commercial shipping vessels. However, America did not publicly announce these strikes. The Pentagon is keeping these occurrences under wraps so as to not demonstrate any intention of resuming major military operations in the region, United States officials told the Wall Street Journal.
The U.S. and Iran have made some “progress” and both Vice President JD Vance and Trump felt “pretty good” about the possibilities for an agreement, the vice president told reporters on Monday.
“Our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran’s demands are reasonable and logical,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters according to Wall Street Journal. “[T]he ball is in the U.S. court.”

sources.text:
The US launched strikes on Iranian targets, a US official said, in what appeared to be a limited operation on the eve of crucial US midterm elections.
Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Unlike earlier in the war, the strikes were not publicly announced.
US President Donald Trump previously said that Washington would not launch strikes on Iran before the midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on US gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress.
Photo: AP
A US official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, on Monday said that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the US in the strait. The move came as Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the critical waterway and resume nuclear talks with the United States.
Back-channel negotiations have also been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than eight-month-old war that has rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Speaking before the US official confirmed strikes, US Vice President J.D. Vance told reporters that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September, but thousands of US troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.
The region is on edge about the prospects of the US resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes are likely to renew concerns.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the US elections, two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter said.
A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week’s elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its blockade on Iran’s ports.
They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from US and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

sources.text:
Over the weekend, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed that President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war “diplomatically” and prefers not to use military force. However, less than 24 hours before the midterm elections, the United States launched airstrikes against Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), citing U.S. officials.
The blasts occurred in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses reported seeing two planes flying over the island, which is located off Iran’s southern coast along the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. officials described the recent strikes as defensive measures, intended to limit Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The reports added that Washington refrained from publicly announcing the strikes to avoid giving the impression that large-scale military operations were resuming. sources.news_title: U.S. Hits Iran Before Midterms as Hormuz Deal Hangs
sources.text:
President Donald Trump confirmed Tuesday that U.S. forces struck an Iranian anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, calling it a "minor attack" that "wasn't a war," hours before voters decided the midterm elections. U.S. officials said the Monday night strike was one of a series of limited, unannounced attacks carried out against Iran in recent weeks, some of them defensive and meant to keep Tehran from threatening commercial ships. Iran answered that the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until the United States meets its conditions. Trump, who said in an interview Monday that he was in "no rush" to decide whether to resume the war, told reporters that "one way or the other, we will do something."
The strike came Monday night, hours after Vice President JD Vance told reporters that he and Trump felt good about the prospects of a negotiated settlement. U.S. officials said a Revolutionary Guard surface-to-air missile had been fired at a U.S. fighter jet and that the response was kept limited, and Trump said the target was an anti-aircraft facility that took Iran about two months to build. Iranian state media reported explosions on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the mainland area of Bandar Abbas, including five blasts in rapid succession on Qeshm. Unlike earlier in the war, the strike was not announced publicly.
Trump had previously said the United States would not strike Iran before the midterm elections, which voters decide on Tuesday, and on Monday he answered "no" when asked whether he was considering a strike afterward, though administration officials say he is still weighing every option. The war and its effect on gasoline prices have been a political vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress. Before the latest reports, the last U.S. attacks publicly known to have been carried out were in early September. Thousands of troops remain in the waters off Iran enforcing a naval blockade, and a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops are on their way to the region.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed to have downed three U.S. drones near Qeshm, a claim U.S. Central Command denied. Iran's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said on state television Tuesday that Tehran had delivered a firm and rational response to the American side, leaving it to Washington to prevent war, without specifying which response he meant. He added that Iran's armed forces remained at their highest level of defensive readiness and warned that another strategic miscalculation would open a new battlefield.
In Tehran on Tuesday, Iran unveiled a massive billboard and banners pledging to kill the U.S. president, and demonstrators gathered in Enghelab Square for a rally calling for revenge, taking the official rhetoric displayed in the capital to a new level. Iranian officials have not said whether the displays were tied to the Qeshm strike, and the rhetoric has not been matched by any change in Iran's negotiating position on the Hormuz reopening plan.
On the diplomatic track, Iran's negotiators had left Qatar with their two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in American hands and no answer yet from Washington, as President Donald Trump warned that the United States might have to "give them the hammer" and reports in Washington and Jerusalem described Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressing for strikes as soon as Tuesday's midterm elections are over. Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, denied that Netanyahu was pressing Trump for strikes. Two Iranian officials said the delegation had ended three days of talks with Qatari mediators in Doha but that messages with the United States continued to pass through the mediator, and a Qatari delegation led by senior official Ali Al Thawadi arrived in Tehran on Monday to meet Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and continue the effort. Araghchi, on a one-day visit to Turkmenistan on Monday, said the outcome now depended on the answers Washington gave to "the Iranian questions." Trump, speaking to reporters Sunday evening, said the war would end "very soon, one way or the other," and that he had held a "very good" call with Netanyahu on Saturday in which Iran was discussed; he gave no details, and Netanyahu's office said nothing. Axios reported that Netanyahu is urging Trump to strike immediately after the vote, and that Trump, with Vice President JD Vance and envoy Steve Witkoff arguing a deal can still be made, is for now leaning toward diplomacy. Two regional officials and a third person briefed on a weekend call between the leaders gave a similar account of Netanyahu's push, and a return to full-scale war would also reshape his options for forming a government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections.
An official briefed on the talks said on Monday that the negotiators had departed on Sunday "not because of difficulties," that a draft proposal was now being circulated and that a follow-up meeting was possible. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the basis remained the seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the strait and end the U.S. naval blockade, now offered on a faster timeline: "No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the U.S. naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran's demands are respected, and Iran's legitimate requirements are addressed." On Tuesday a senior Iranian official said Iran and the United States remained far from a deal, that mediators were working to narrow the gaps and that Tehran's conditions must be met if Washington wants Hormuz reopened. The official added that talks on Iran's nuclear program could begin only after those conditions were fulfilled and that Tehran would not accept what it called excessive demands. Trump had found a reason to sound hopeful on Monday. "Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran," he wrote on Truth Social. "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" At the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, closing his midterm campaign, he said "it's not a war" and that he hoped it would not weigh on voters "when they go into the voting booth." Tehran's framing was the mirror image: Baghaei said "the ball is in the U.S. court," and Araghchi, in remarks carried by IRNA, said the mediated talks were "proceeding very intensively" but that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality."
The standoff hardened over a weekend that began with Trump telling reporters on Saturday that negotiations were "going fine," that Iran was "not very reliable" and that the United States was "not in that much of a hurry" to reach a deal. Tehran's reply came not through the mediators but on state television and in the streets: footage of missiles and drones being hauled out of underground storage, a civil defense commander describing how the power grid would be partitioned to survive bombing, and a security chief setting out, line by line, what the United States would have to concede before Iran reopened the waterway or discussed its nuclear program at all.
The result, on the eve of the U.S. midterm elections that Trump had set as the boundary for any resumption of strikes, was a negotiation in which both capitals said the other must move first and neither had publicly moved before Monday night's limited strikes. Iran's offer, which Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described to Al Jazeera on Saturday, is now the only concrete text either side has acknowledged: a reopening of the strait within two days, down from the seven-day plan carried by Qatar a week earlier, if Iran's conditions are met. The U.S. draft that Qatari mediators brought to Tehran on Friday has not been published, and the letter Vice President JD Vance sent to Iran's top security official a week ago remains, by that official's own account, unanswered. Araghchi told parliament's national security committee on Sunday that the Qatari side had first proposed cutting Iran's seven-day timetable to five days before Tehran offered two, and that a meeting with an American delegation was not on the agenda at this stage.
Trump spoke to reporters for about 11 minutes on Saturday night amid costumed guests at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach. Asked about the talks, he said they were "going fine" but that Iran was "not very reliable." He said the United States had "knocked out their nuclear" capability but added: "We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes." He referred to Pickaxe Mountain, the underground site near Natanz that U.S. officials have described as unfinished, and said the United States had a plan for it. He also said Washington had no fixed timetable: "We're not in that much of a hurry." On the question of a deal, he said: "Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They want to make a deal; we'll find out about that."
The remarks landed on top of a day in which Iran had sent its most detailed signal yet of what a settlement would require. Araghchi, speaking to Al Jazeera while an Iranian delegation sat with Qatari mediators in Doha, called the Vance letter "a positive step" and said Iran could reopen Hormuz within two days rather than seven if its conditions were tangibly implemented. On Saturday night Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and the addressee of the Vance letter, told state television that Washington's "tone has completely changed," which he called a good sign, and then set out what Iran wants in sequence. The United States must lift the naval blockade that has halted Iran's oil exports and most of its trade through its southern ports. It must issue waivers for oil sanctions. It must unfreeze Iran's assets abroad. It must stop fighting on every regional front, including Lebanon. And it must recognize a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement governing passage through the strait. Until those steps are taken, Rezaei said, transit in the strait and surrounding waters would not return to normal and there would be no talks on Iran's nuclear program. He said he had not yet replied to Vance. He also said there had been no decision to change Iran's nuclear doctrine, while acknowledging that some Iranians had asked whether it should change if the country were attacked again.
By Sunday the Iranian government had added that it was awaiting the American response. Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based analyst described in Iranian and regional media as close to Rezaei, wrote on X that if the conditions were not met the letter would likely go unanswered and negotiations, including on the nuclear file, would not move to a higher level. "It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands," he wrote. "It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, hosting Group of 20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, said Saturday that Trump "hasn't made a decision" on resuming strikes and preferred a diplomatic resolution. He has also said he did not know whether the Qatar-led talks had a timeframe. Pakistan's military, which is running a parallel mediation track, said after its own meetings in Tehran that it was "cautiously optimistic."
Iran's leadership spent Sunday making sure the diplomatic offer was not read as weakness. State media aired footage of missiles and drones being brought out of large underground storage complexes and deployed, presented as a record of the eight months of war. Gholamreza Jalali, who heads the National Organization for Passive Defense, said in a speech that his agency had identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need protection if the war restarted, and that officials were considering "network islanding," the practice of splitting the grid into segments so that a strike on one would not black out the others. He did not name the sectors. The subtext was plain: Tehran expects that if the United States hits again, its power grid will be among the targets, and it is preparing to absorb that rather than to prevent it.
The posture follows directly from Saturday's statement by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who convened the commanders of the Revolutionary Guard, the regular army and the general staff and ordered that any threat be met with an immediate response "without geographical limitations," urging the commanders to expand the list of potential targets. Iranian officials have said in recent weeks that if the country's civilian infrastructure is attacked again, undersea cables and other regional infrastructure could become targets. The army's spokesman, Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia, warned Friday on X that a resumption of U.S. operations would draw a far wider region into the war. Officials quoted by Iranian media over the weekend said Iran could inflict "devastating strikes" on American warships in the region and that any force attempting a ground landing would find a "killing ground," language that Al Jazeera's live coverage on Sunday paired with a claim that the Iranian military's "epic resilience" had brought the United States and its allies to "the hard wall of reality."
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, wrote that Araghchi's two-day offer showed some flexibility on sequencing that could let both sides claim an initial achievement without resolving their core dispute, but that the military statements "show the limits of this opening." Tehran, he said, appears determined to avoid a repeat of earlier rounds in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed strikes, and its objective is to make another attack costly and unpredictable enough that Washington reconsiders it altogether. Negar Mortazavi of the Center for International Policy put the problem more simply to Al Jazeera: Iran wants a series of concessions, the United States wants progress on the nuclear program before it concedes anything, and "each side wants the other to act first."
None of the weekend's words changed anything on the water, where the Revolutionary Guard continues to enforce its own rules. At least four tankers were identified as struck on Friday and Saturday, according to monitoring compiled by Al Jazeera, with the caveat that not every attack is reported by ships or trackers. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center reported that a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas was hit by three projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island, well inside the Gulf, with the crew safe. On Sunday afternoon, Iran's navy claimed through the semi-official Fars news agency that a "violating oil tanker" transiting a prohibited area east of the strait had ignored warnings and caught fire after striking sea mines. The claim could not be independently verified. Iran has now asserted that nearly 10 ships have hit mines while using the southern channel along the Omani coast, the route the U.S. Navy has escorted tankers through since July.
The American account remains the opposite. Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of Central Command, said again Friday that Iran's navy was no longer patrolling the strait after U.S. strikes earlier in the year, that he had flown the length of the waterway during the week without seeing an Iranian warship, and that the lanes were clear of Iranian mines. CENTCOM has called the Guard's mine-strike claims false. As HNGN reported Saturday, the two versions are reconciled by the numbers: UKMTO logged just over 30 reported attacks in October, the most of any month in the war, and the strait is carrying a fraction of its prewar traffic. Maritime trackers citing IMF PortWatch data recorded two transits on October 25 against a pre-crisis baseline of about 85 a day. Whatever the state of Iran's patrol fleet, the threat of what happens to ships that use an unapproved route is enough to keep most owners and insurers on the Iranian-sanctioned one.
A U.S. Treasury Department assessment prepared to inform Trump's decision, reported by Axios, offers the clearest public picture of what the blockade has done. No new oil has been loaded onto tankers at Iran's export terminals since August 25, the report said. Overseas crude deliveries have fallen. Iran's year-on-year inflation approached 90 percent in September, and the rial continued to slide. The report described the economy as "crippled" by the combination of the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation, the campaign the administration calls Operation Economic Outcast. It did not conclude that the economy was close to collapse.
That distinction matters for both sides' calculations. Trump's "not in a hurry" rests on a belief, which the Treasury numbers support, that time is working against Tehran. Rezaei's insistence on blockade relief as the first step rests on the same reading. The two-day plan is, in effect, Iran's bid to convert the strait, the one lever it still fully holds, into relief from the lever it cannot escape. Araghchi's price list on Saturday was explicit about that trade: sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum lifted, oil waivers restored, frozen funds released including those held in Qatar, and a recognized shipping route agreed with Oman, with other routes closed. Nuclear proposals from the mediators, he said, were being reviewed as a second phase. Vance's letter, as reported by the New York Times, proposed direct talks with the nuclear program on the table from the first session. The sequencing dispute has not narrowed; it has only been stated more precisely by both sides.
The weekend fixed the shape of the choice Trump will face after Tuesday. U.S. and allied officials have told reporters for a week that strike options would be presented to the president after the midterm elections, and Trump had said publicly that he would not attack before November 3; Monday night's strike, which Trump described Tuesday as a minor attack and which was not announced, came before that date. He has now said, in the same breath, that talks are fine, that he is in no hurry, and that the remaining targets could be dealt with in minutes. Each statement is consistent with a different course, and the administration has not said which it intends. Iran has answered the ambiguity by making its own choice visible: a reopening offer that is real but conditional, and a military posture built around preemption rather than retaliation. Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, chief of Iran's general staff, said Saturday that the armed forces "will not wait" for a confirmed hostile action to begin before choosing the time and manner of their response.
For the Gulf states, whose territory absorbed Iranian retaliation in earlier rounds and whose airports and energy facilities have been hit by the Houthis in parallel, the stakes are immediate. The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have warned several regional governments that military action after the midterms could draw Iranian strikes on their soil. Saudi air defenses intercepted a drone over the Riyadh region on Saturday, the coalition said, and Houthi attacks on Yemen's government in Aden continued into the weekend. At the Manama Dialogue in Bahrain, the annual security summit organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, the mood was openly grim. "We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," said Anwar Gargash, the Emirati presidential adviser, who conceded that "the rules of logic" showed the American and Iranian positions far apart and that "if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst." Egypt's foreign minister, Badr Abdelatty, told the same gathering that "the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere." Saudi Vice Foreign Minister Waleed ElKhereiji said efforts were under way to prevent an escalation, and the Gulf Cooperation Council's secretary-general said Arab states remained open to talks with Iran but needed a reciprocal response from Tehran. The institute's own tally gives the warning its weight: the United Arab Emirates has faced more than 3,000 Iranian drones and ballistic missiles aimed at airports, military and oil facilities since February, most of them intercepted, and Gulf governments have spent billions on air defense since. China, which has stayed out of the mediation so far, said Monday it would send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November; President Xi Jinping told Oman's sultan that the Gulf "should not become an arena for great-power rivalry."
For the broader diplomatic calendar, the Iran question now sits beside another: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff has confirmed that Washington will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11, and the Kremlin has said a Russian delegation will attend. If both tracks hold, the administration will be negotiating the end of two wars in the same weeks it decides whether to resume one.
What comes next runs on two tracks, and the first has a date. Tuesday's midterm elections are the line Trump has drawn for any resumption of major strikes, and officials have said the options will be on his desk once the votes are in. Until then the clearest signal of Iran's intent is whether Rezaei answers the Vance letter, and whether any answer accepts direct talks with the nuclear program on the agenda from the first session. The New York Times has reported that such talks could begin as early as this week in Qatar or Turkey if Tehran agrees; Araghchi said Sunday that such a meeting was not on the agenda at this stage, and that Iran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy."
The second track is the water itself. Oil markets read the weekend as a step toward a deal rather than away from one: Brent fell 7.6 percent on Monday, losing $8.66 to settle at $104.77 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate slipped below $100, with little behind the move beyond the fact that the talks had not collapsed. On Tuesday Brent edged back up to roughly $105 to $106 after reports of the Qeshm strike. A reopening of the strait would show up in UKMTO's incident reports and the daily transit count before it appeared in any statement from either capital, and the October figures, the highest of the war, are the baseline against which the two-day plan will be judged. Iran's other preparation is also visible: a government that spends a Sunday explaining how it will keep the lights on under bombardment is telling Washington what it expects the next target set to be, and that it intends to be standing when it is over. Whether the Qeshm strike, which Trump called minor, was a one-off answer to missile fire or the latest step in a quieter campaign that officials say has been under way for weeks is now the question, and for the first time both sides have said aloud that they can wait.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report the strikes, which a US official characterized as a “defensive measure” in response to Iran’s use of surface-to-air missiles against American forces that have been waging a war against Iran since February.

The US military did not publicly announce the attack on Qeshm Island, which came hours before American voters were set to head to the polls to decide whether President Donald Trump’s party should remain in control of Congress.
The Journal reported that the Trump administration had “purposefully” been keeping its recent campaign of smaller-scale strikes on Iran quiet “so as not to signal any intention of resuming major combat operations.”
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tuesday that “Iran is prepared for any scenario” and stressed that the country “retains its right to legitimate self-defense until the military aggression has been brought to a complete and permanent end.”
Last month, Trump vowed that the US would “not be attacking Iran at any time prior” to the midterms and that the two sides were engaged in “productive discussions.”
Vice President JD Vance asserted Monday that he and Trump “both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement” to end the massively unpopular and destructive war with Iran.

Murphy, whose remarks were based on information he and other lawmakers received during a classified briefing, did not specifically warn that Trump was considering the use of nuclear weapons against Iran.

“Whether these allegations reflect serious military planning or reckless posturing, the very possibility of a US nuclear attack on Iran is an unconscionable horror,” NIAC said in response.

THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do)
- American forces struck Iranian targets on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz Monday after Iranian forces reportedly fired on a U.S. aircraft.
- U.S. officials described the operation as defensive — and revealed that other limited American strikes had been conducted in recent weeks without public announcements.
- The strikes came as Trump said a peace deal “could happen,” with Iran offering conditional terms for reopening the vital oil-shipping corridor.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time)
President Trump says Iran wants a deal.
American forces, meanwhile, just bombed part of Iran.
And if that wasn’t enough Election Eve excitement, U.S. officials say this wasn’t even the first recent American strike that Washington chose not to announce.
There’s diplomacy, there’s military pressure, and then there’s whatever happens when both arrive at the same address.
On Monday evening, American forces carried out limited airstrikes against Iranian targets on Qeshm Island, a strategically important piece of Iranian territory at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
Multiple American officials confirmed the operation to the Associated Press, CBS News and other outlets.
One senior military official told CBS News the operation followed Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces firing at an American aircraft.
Other officials described the strikes as targeting Iranian surface-to-air missile capabilities threatening U.S. assets.
The strikes were characterized as defensive rather than the beginning of another major American air campaign.
But here’s the detail that deserves considerably more attention.
U.S. officials also acknowledged that American forces had conducted other limited strikes in recent weeks without publicly announcing them.
According to reporting by The Washington Post and ABC News, the decision not to publicize some operations was intended to avoid suggesting that Washington had resumed major combat operations against Iran.
In other words, the public was hearing about diplomatic maneuvering while limited military exchanges were continuing behind the scenes.
The latest confrontation reportedly followed an incident involving American aircraft.
Iranian authorities also claimed Monday to have shot down two American RQ-170 reconnaissance drones. A U.S. official disputed that claim.
Iranian state media subsequently reported explosions on Qeshm Island.
U.S. Central Command had not provided a detailed public account of the strike when the reports emerged.
The location matters.
Qeshm Island sits along the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
It’s one of the world’s most important energy-shipping routes.
When military tensions threaten traffic through the strait, the consequences aren’t confined to admirals, diplomats and Pentagon briefing rooms.
They can reach American gasoline pumps, shipping companies and household budgets.
And that brings us to the political timing.
The strikes took place on the eve of America’s midterm elections, with the Iran conflict already a major issue in the campaign.
Trump has been trying to demonstrate that he can bring the confrontation toward a negotiated conclusion.
On Monday, he suggested an agreement remained possible.
A deal “could happen,” the president wrote on Truth Social.
He added: “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.”
Vice President JD Vance offered a similarly optimistic assessment.
“We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more,” Vance told reporters.
Iran’s government, however, presented a more conditional picture.
Tehran indicated it might reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if Washington accepted its terms.
Iranian officials also suggested the responsibility for moving negotiations forward rested with the United States.
Qatar has been helping mediate indirect negotiations, but Monday’s reports indicated that several days of talks had not produced a decisive breakthrough.
So the situation is rather delicate.
The United States wants Iran to stop threatening shipping and American assets.
Iran wants relief from American pressure and guarantees regarding any agreement.
Israel, meanwhile, is worried about leaving Iran with the capacity to threaten the region again.
According to Associated Press reporting, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to consider additional military action.
Other regional governments fear another large-scale campaign could ignite a much broader conflict involving Iranian-aligned forces.
And American officials are balancing all of that while attempting to keep the strategic waterway open.
The administration has maintained a naval blockade and deployed additional military forces to the region.
The conflict has already carried enormous economic and military costs.
Oil prices fell sharply Monday as financial markets reacted to the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough.
But markets were welcoming talk of peace on the very same day that American aircraft were attacking Iranian military targets.
That’s quite a split-screen.
For American voters, the central question is no longer whether the United States might someday become involved in another confrontation with Iran.
The country is already involved in military operations, and the administration is simultaneously trying to negotiate a way out of the current crisis.
Monday’s strikes underline the considerable distance between optimistic diplomatic announcements and the situation facing American personnel in the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump is saying Iran wants a settlement.
Iran is setting conditions.
American forces are answering missile threats with airstrikes.
And the voters are being asked to decide which party they trust with the next chapter.
Whatever happens at the negotiating table, one thing is already clear.
The Strait of Hormuz hasn’t gotten the memo that it’s Election Day.

sources.news_title: Oil Prices Rise After Reports of Explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island
sources.text:
Oil prices climbed by more than 1.5 percent early on Nov. 3 after reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures rose by $1.84, or 1.76 percent, to $106.61 a barrel by 2:44 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.60, or 1.66 percent, to $98.06.
Earlier on Nov. 2, Iranian state media IRNA reported several explosions on Qeshm Island, the biggest island in the Persian Gulf.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Nov. 3 confirmed U.S. strikes on an Iranian anti-aircraft facility on the night of Nov. 2.
Speaking to Fox News’s “Fox & Friends,” Trump said the U.S. military hit the facility shortly after its completion.
“They have no airplanes. They have no anti-aircraft. We took some out last night. It’s just a minor attack. It wasn’t war,” Trump said. “They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built, as soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely.”
Asked about the reported explosions on Qeshm Island, a U.S. official told The Epoch Times that Trump “has all options available at any time.”
“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the U.S. official said.
The Epoch Times reached out to U.S. Central Command for further comment but didn’t receive a response by the time of publication.
On Nov. 2, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social that oil prices were “dropping like a rock” because markets believed that war with Iran could be avoided.
“Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” he wrote.
Trump also said Washington still needed to address one or two remaining Iranian nuclear sites, including the suspected underground nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
Iranian officials said on Nov. 2 that indirect diplomatic contacts with the United States were continuing but described the issues under discussion as highly complicated.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Iran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz unless Washington lifted the naval blockade imposed in July.
Shipping Risks
Maritime security risks remain high in the Strait of Hormuz despite a modest recovery in shipping activity.
On Nov. 1, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said it had received a report that a vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz after another ship relayed a mayday call.
UKMTO advised vessels to transit with caution while authorities investigated.
According to S&P Global Commodities at Sea, vessel traffic through the Strait reached its highest monthly level since July in October, supported by stronger liquefied natural gas and dry-bulk movements despite lower crude tanker volumes.
The Nov. 2 report said the operating environment had become increasingly volatile, citing reported projectile strikes, vessel fires, and other security incidents throughout October.
International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said there had been about 30 attacks during the month—among the highest monthly totals recorded.
While Iranian aerial attacks continued to pose risks to shipping, Dominguez warned that uncertainty over the possible presence of naval mines remained a major concern.
“I cannot guarantee that it’s safe,” he told reporters on Nov. 2. “That’s why we are not recommending anyone to go through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Despite the heightened security environment, S&P Global data showed total observed and estimated vessel transits through Hormuz edged up to 750 in October from 749 in September, although very large crude carrier movements declined to 156 from 184 during the same period.

U.S. forces carried out new defensive strikes against Iranian targets on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz as President Trump’s administration continued working toward a possible negotiated settlement with Tehran.
The strikes targeted military threats in one of the most strategically important waterways in the world. American officials stressed that the action did not mark a return to full-scale combat operations.
That combination—military pressure without abandoning diplomacy—is the clearest sign yet of the narrow path President Trump is trying to hold.
Reuters confirmed the location of the U.S. action:

— Reuters (@Reuters) November 3, 2026
Qeshm Island sits at the northern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint through which a major share of the world’s oil moves. Any missile launch site or air-defense position there can threaten American forces, allied assets and commercial shipping.
ABC News reports that U.S. officials described the strikes as limited and defensive. The officials said the operation was intended to protect American assets in the region and did not signal the resumption of a broader bombing campaign.
Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm and nearby Hengam Island, along with activity around Bandar Abbas on the mainland. No reliable casualty figure had been released when this article was published.
The outlet also placed the attack against the backdrop of more than eight months of conflict, disrupted shipping and back-channel diplomacy. That context is important because the new strike was presented as a response to a specific military threat, not an announcement that Washington had abandoned the negotiating track or opened a new unrestricted phase of the war.
Another current report framed the action as a defensive response near the strait:
US conducts defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating tensions in the Middle East.https://t.co/ep5ROKGCND pic.twitter.com/KUjNA8aErS
— Gulf News (@gulf_news) November 3, 2026
The timing is remarkable because the military action came alongside public signs that negotiations may be moving in a better direction.
Vice President JD Vance told reporters that he and President Trump felt good about the prospects for a negotiated settlement after what he called a number of productive conversations.
Axios reports that President Trump said he was in no rush to order a wider bombing campaign. He later pointed to falling oil prices as evidence that markets increasingly believe a new war may be avoided and wrote that a settlement with Iran “could happen.”
Vice President Vance said he had spoken with President Trump about the talks and that both men felt good about the prospect of reaching a settlement. Oil prices had dropped sharply as the diplomatic effort gained attention, giving the administration an immediate economic reason to keep pressing for a durable agreement rather than a temporary pause.
Those words do not amount to a signed agreement. Iran has demanded sanctions relief and a wider ceasefire arrangement, while American officials have not announced a final package or a timetable for completing one.
A president who can strike a military target threatening U.S. assets while still keeping a diplomatic channel alive is operating from strength, not confusion.
A third report identified the target as a missile launch platform:
🇺🇸🇮🇷⚡- The US struck a missile launch platform on Qeshm Island, Iran, officials tell CNN. https://t.co/21Yj5XrkYc
— Rerum Novarum // Intel, Breaking News, and Alerts (@officialrnintel) November 3, 2026
CBS News reports that the diplomatic effort has included discussions involving regional intermediaries while U.S. officials monitor continuing threats around the Strait of Hormuz. The talks remain fluid, and neither Washington nor Tehran has announced a completed deal.
The negotiations are unfolding while American forces remain exposed to missile threats and commercial traffic continues moving through a chokepoint vital to global energy markets. That leaves the administration balancing three immediate priorities: protecting U.S. personnel, keeping the waterway open, and preventing a limited defensive operation from becoming a wider war.
That uncertainty is exactly why American military readiness still matters. Negotiations backed by empty warnings invite delay and deception.
Negotiations backed by the demonstrated ability to neutralize a threat are very different.
The administration also has to guard against escalation. A defensive strike can protect American forces without committing the country to another open-ended war, but only if the mission remains disciplined and the objectives stay clear.
President Trump has repeatedly said he wants a settlement that protects American interests and prevents Iran from threatening the region. The developments around Qeshm show that he is willing to use force when necessary while still leaving Tehran a path away from a much larger conflict.
That is the right order: protect Americans, keep the pressure on, and make the other side choose whether it wants a deal or the consequences of refusing one.

The US has launched fresh strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, officials have said, just hours before Americans head to the polls in midterm elections that could reshape the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency.
Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on the island on Monday, while Iranian state television also reported blasts. A US official, speaking anonymously because they were not authorised to comment publicly, said the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets.
The attacks were described by US officials as limited in scope and were said to be a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft. They did not appear to signal a return to full-scale hostilities.
The timing is politically sensitive for Trump. The midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress or Democrats take power in one or both chambers, potentially making it harder for the president to advance his legislative agenda.
The conflict with Iran, and its impact on petrol prices and the wider US economy, has emerged as a vulnerability for Republicans seeking to hold on to their congressional majorities.
Trump had previously indicated that the US would not launch fresh strikes before election day. Asked on Monday whether Washington would resume attacks after the midterms, he replied: “No”.
Earlier, however, the president told reporters he was in “no rush” to escalate military action against Tehran.
“One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially,” he told Axios. “They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it.”
The latest strikes underline the delicate balance facing the White House as Trump seeks to maintain pressure on Iran while avoiding a wider conflict with potentially significant consequences for energy markets and the domestic political landscape.
With control of Congress at stake, any escalation risks further exposing Republicans to criticism over the economic costs of the war.
Trump could be days away from authorising a nuclear strike against Iran, Tucker Carlson has claimed, warning that pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu risks triggering a catastrophic global conflict.
The former Fox News presenter alleged that Netanyahu is urging the US president to use nuclear weapons against Pickaxe Mountain, an underground Iranian facility where Israeli intelligence reportedly believes Tehran has resumed uranium enrichment.
In a lengthy post on X, Carlson claimed the Trump administration could be approaching a decision with potentially devastating consequences.
“Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran,” he wrote.
Carlson argued that the facility, buried beneath approximately 300 feet of solid granite, could not be destroyed using conventional American weapons.
“No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike,” he claimed.
He added that an unnamed source had told him: “Bibi calls Trump about it every day.”
The allegations come as speculation grows over whether Washington will resume major military operations against Tehran following this week’s US midterm elections. Carlson claimed Trump could decide by November 7 whether to authorise a nuclear attack, although there is no independently verified evidence that such a decision is being considered.
Neither the White House nor the Israeli government has confirmed Carlson’s claims. Trump also said in an October 16 interview that he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran, adding: “I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to.”

US strikes in the Strait of Hormuz create more questions about what’s ahead
What appeared to be a limited strike by the United States on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday’s midterm U.S. elections is raising questions about what’s coming next.
For weeks now, U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the elections. Just days ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed military action, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
Talks aimed at avoiding that are ongoing, and other American allies in the region are pressuring the U.S. not to resume the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress.
Strikes were targeted in Strait of Hormuz
Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
A U.S. official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait.
Iran official says US must resolve its conditions
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said Tuesday that the U.S. response to Tehran’s demands to end the war was not convincing.
Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei wrote on social media that the strait won’t reopen until the U.S. addresses Iran’s conditions.
Iran has offered to reopen the strait, and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire including in Lebanon.
Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement
Back-channel negotiations have been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump.
Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.
Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a call with Trump over the weekend, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the strait in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade.
The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has called on Iran and the U.S. to engage in dialogue and reach an agreement to resolve their ongoing conflict, warning against further military escalation in the region.
Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections
Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies.
“The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children,” said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei.
One woman was less optimistic.
“It doesn’t really make much difference who comes into power,” said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. “The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I’m not talking about the American people, mind you. I’m talking about their policies.”
Iran’s chief negotiator says it’s up to the US to prevent renewed war
Iranian state television quoted the country’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had “delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war.” It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to.
Qalibaf also warned that Iran’s armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness.
“If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today,” he said.

Oil prices dropped on Tuesday evening following a sharp rise in the morning after reports of a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island revived concerns about an escalation of the conflict and further disruption at the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, was trading 1.72 per cent lower at $102.97 a barrel at 6:16pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was down 1.03 per cent to 95.47 a barrel.
Both benchmarks rose sharply earlier in the day, with Brent reaching nearly $107 a barrel. The gains followed a sharp slide on Monday, when both Brent and WTI plunged more than 7 per cent.
US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday night, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday. The WSJ cited US officials, who described the attacks as defensive measures aimed at preventing Iran from targeting commercial vessels in the strait.
Iranian state media said there were several explosions on the island, which is at the mouth of Hormuz. It was the latest in a series of limited attacks carried out by the US in recent weeks, the WSJ report said.
Smaller scale strikes have been carried out and kept secret to avoid indicating any US intent to resume its major military campaign against Iran, the report added.
“Overnight US strikes renewed uncertainty, leaving crude near $105 per barrel this morning and the diplomatic opening vulnerable,” said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD.
The latest military action comes as the US goes to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections. It also puts the focus back on the risk of supply disruption, a day after US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wanted to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes.
“For oil, the decisive question will be whether the midterm elections can align the political pieces to pave the way for more normal supply conditions – or push that prospect further away,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote.
“The clearest downside scenario for crude is credible de-escalation of geopolitical tensions followed by improving supply flows. The clearest upside scenario is renewed disruption while inventories continue absorbing the shortfall.”
While the US midterms could change expectations rapidly, “they cannot, by themselves, reopen shipping routes, repair damaged infrastructure or reverse the AI impact on broader economies”, she added.
The Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route connecting the Gulf to global markets, carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas supplies before the conflict began in late February.
Oil prices hit a six-month high at the end of October on Hormuz strikes and the probability of the conflict escalating again after the midterm elections.
"Energy prices have been at lofty levels for a while, at least from our perspective. Oil trading above $100 and European natural gas above €90 is difficult to reconcile with current market realities," said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer.
"We are in an extraordinarily noisy week due to the midterms, and in a phase where the complex energy supply chains are normalising. Given this setting, today’s exceptional market fever and wild price swings should not come as a surprise. We maintain our cautious view on oil."

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — The U.S. military carried out limited airstrikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, Nov. 2, targeting military positions reportedly threatening American aircraft and other assets as the Trump administration continued negotiations aimed at ending the war with Iran.
Three American officials confirmed the operation to CBS News, describing the attacks as defensive rather than the beginning of a renewed large-scale military campaign. The strikes targeted Iran’s Qeshm Island, a strategically important position near the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with international shipping routes.
Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near the mainland port city of Bandar Abbas. American officials did not immediately disclose the number of targets struck, the weapons employed or whether Iranian military personnel were killed or injured.
According to ABC News, one U.S. official said Monday’s operation followed an Iranian attack against an American aircraft. Earlier that day, Iranian authorities claimed to have shot down two American RQ-170 reconnaissance drones, an assertion a U.S. official disputed.
Another American official told The Associated Press that the strikes targeted Iranian personnel using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets in the strait. The official, who spoke anonymously because the operation had not been publicly announced, characterized the military action as limited.
The airstrikes were carried out one day before the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections, despite President Donald Trump’s earlier statements that American forces would not launch new attacks against Iran before voting concluded. Unlike major operations conducted earlier in the conflict, the administration did not immediately announce the latest strikes, and U.S. Central Command had not issued a detailed public account.
American officials also acknowledged that U.S. forces have conducted additional limited strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks without public announcements. Those operations reportedly focused on reducing threats to American military assets and commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf.
The operation comes amid a conflict that began Feb. 28 with joint American and Israeli strikes against Iran. Although large-scale U.S. attacks had subsided, American forces have maintained a naval blockade intended to prevent Iranian oil shipments from reaching international markets. Thousands of U.S. personnel remain deployed near Iran, with another aircraft carrier and additional reinforcements reportedly heading to the region.
The Strait of Hormuz remains central to the conflict because approximately one-fifth of the world’s oil supply ordinarily passes through the waterway. Iranian attacks on commercial vessels and threats to shipping have disrupted maritime traffic, contributed to rising energy costs and complicated efforts to restore regional trade. A tanker was struck near Oman on Friday, forcing the evacuation of 25 crew members, according to The Washington Post.
Despite Monday’s military action, Washington and Tehran have continued pursuing a negotiated settlement through regional mediators. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump remained optimistic about diplomacy following discussions with Iranian representatives.
Speaking to reporters after returning to Washington, Vance said he and the president “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
Qatar has been working with both governments on proposals involving the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, restrictions on Iranian attacks against shipping and the possible removal of the American naval blockade. Iranian officials have indicated that the waterway could reopen within two days if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions, although major disagreements remain over sanctions, maritime control and security guarantees.
According to Al Jazeera’s Nov. 3 reporting, Iranian military officials are demanding an end to regional hostilities, the removal of economic sanctions, access to frozen Iranian assets and guarantees against future military attacks. Tehran has also called for recognition of its authority over the Strait of Hormuz, a position that would raise significant questions about international navigation rights.
Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, responded to the American strikes Tuesday by asserting Tehran’s right to defend itself until military attacks cease. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, who has participated in negotiations, also warned that the country’s armed forces remained prepared for renewed hostilities.
“The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war,” Qalibaf said, according to Iranian state television.
The strikes also occurred amid pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for additional American military action. Regional officials familiar with recent discussions said Netanyahu urged Trump during a weekend telephone conversation to consider another sustained campaign against Iranian targets following the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump has alternated between expressing confidence in a diplomatic agreement and warning that further strikes remain possible if negotiations fail. On Monday, he suggested that Iran wanted an agreement but later indicated during a Fox News appearance that American forces might still target additional military or nuclear facilities.
The continuing conflict has imposed substantial financial costs on the United States. According to CBS News’ review of U.S. Central Command estimates, military expenditures had reached at least $47.1 billion by mid-October, including approximately $29 billion to replace expended munitions, $6.1 billion for lost equipment and $11.9 billion in additional operational expenses. Those figures exclude damage to American military installations in the region.
Monday’s airstrikes underscore the continuing risk of renewed escalation despite ongoing negotiations. While U.S. officials described the operation as a limited defensive response to threats against American assets, Iran has maintained that further attacks could jeopardize diplomatic progress and trigger additional retaliation. Neither government has announced a final agreement, leaving the future of the Strait of Hormuz and the broader military confrontation unresolved.

sources.news_title: Iran Strikes and US Midterms: Market Reactions and Impact
sources.text:
London, 3 November 2026 — EBM Newsdesk Analysis — By Anthony Gill
America votes today, and Donald Trump has chosen to go into the midterms with a show of force. New US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island overnight have put geopolitics back at the centre of the markets, at a moment when investors were already nervous about the tech sell-off.
London’s FTSE 100 is expected to open lower. Across Asia, the selling has become serious enough that Beijing has stepped in.
A Show of Strength Before the Vote
The Qeshm strikes appear limited, but they cut against the message of diplomacy the White House had been pushing in recent weeks. The timing looks deliberate. Trump’s approval rating has slipped as the conflict has dragged on and petrol prices have stayed painfully high. Being seen to hold the upper hand on polling day was clearly too tempting.

Oil reacted, but not dramatically. Brent rose about 2% to above $106 a barrel. That is a long way below the $125 peak seen in April, and the modest move shows traders still expect talks to prevent a bigger escalation. For Europe, which is already paying for a war it isn’t fighting through higher energy and transport costs, any rise in crude feeds straight back into inflation.
Blue Wave or Ripple?
The polls point to a strong night for the Democrats, possibly including control of the Senate. But Republican support has been underestimated before, and markets are not pricing in a certain outcome.
One issue cuts across party lines: data centres. Voters on both sides are worried about the power bills, water use and land taken by the AI build-out. If the result signals political pressure to slow that expansion, it lands on tech stocks that are already struggling.
Apple Wins by Not Spending
Wall Street’s short rebound has faded. Investors remain uneasy about the huge sums being spent on AI infrastructure without clear evidence of returns, a concern that has dragged global markets into the red in recent weeks.
Apple has largely avoided the damage, mainly because it never joined the AI spending race. Its latest results beat expectations, with strong iPhone sales lifting revenue. But China sales were weaker than forecast and iPad demand fell short. The shares ended flat after hours. Apple did well, but not well enough for a market that now expects perfection.
Beijing Steps In
The biggest story is in Asia. Chip stocks have fallen sharply, and China has responded by quietly halting new listings. The China Securities Regulatory Commission has reportedly told banks informally to delay new IPOs and large share sales until markets stabilise. The People’s Bank of China has also announced new support measures.
The move follows a bruising October. The CSI 300 index fell 8.5% last month, its worst month in more than a decade. Beijing clearly fears that a tech-led sell-off could become a wider loss of confidence in the economy.
But the move may backfire. China has spent years encouraging companies to list at home and trying to deepen its capital markets. Shutting the door on new listings tells investors that regulators are worried, and that can make the selling worse rather than better.
My Read
Today’s three stories share a common thread: governments trying to control outcomes they can’t fully control. Trump wants strength without a wider war. Voters want AI without the power bills. Beijing wants rising share prices without real confidence behind them.
China’s IPO freeze may buy a few calm weeks, but it does nothing about the bigger questions: a weak Chinese economy and whether the hundreds of billions going into AI will ever pay off. Restricting the supply of shares can slow a sell-off, but it can’t end one. Until investors see real returns from AI and a path out of the Iran conflict, markets will stay nervous.
